replying_to: Replying to Doc-to-LoRA: Learning to Instantly Internalize Contexts
display_title: Official Review of Submission9692 by Reviewer x6RM

summary.value: This work points out that the quadratic attention cost of the Transformer is expensive. Therefore, this work proposes the Doc-to-LoRA (D2L), which meta-learns to perform approximate context distillation in a single forward pass. According to the experimental results, the model achieves about 4x the training context window.

strengths.value:
* The idea is interesting. This work uses D2L Hypernet to process the chunks, and then uses the weights of each document to the LLM to generate the response.
* The paper is written clearly. Figure 1 presents the pipeline of the training process and the data construction. The method part describes how to create and use the activation.
* The experiment supports that the Doc-Lora could have great performance, with a few additional costs.
* This work provides the pseudo-code for the Doc-to-Lora, making the reproduction easy.
* The prompt is provided for reproduction.

weaknesses.value:
* The baseline may be missed. This work does not compare the performance with other text-to-weight works.
* This work uses gemma for the experiment. It is not clear whether the claim is still the same as other models.
* It is not clear how the performance is on the distribution dataset. For example, if you train on PwC and test on SQuAD, what is the performance.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission9692 by Reviewer x6RM

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their overall positive sentiment towards the paper. We also thank the reviewer for commenting on the paper as ***having an interesting idea*** and ***clear writing***. We are also glad to hear that ***D2L could have great performance with a few additional costs*** and ***that our content facilitates easy reproduction***.

Here, we address the concerns and questions raised by the reviewer.

---

> This work uses gemma for the experiment. It is not clear whether the claim is still the same as other models.


We have added results for ***Mistral-7B and Qwen3-4B in Appendix E (Figure 9-12)*** of the revised paper. The trends and conclusions are largely similar to the results reported using the gemma2-2B model.

Furthermore, we have added an experiment where the ***context encoder is replaced with a VLM (gemma-3-4b-it) while the target model is a pure text model (gemma-2-2b-it) in Section 5.2*** of the revised paper. To test whether the target model can classify images based solely on the internalized information, we use the Imagenette dataset, a 10-class subset of ImageNet. The target model is prompted with the following text: “*What is in this image? Choose exactly one of the following classes: tench, English springer, cassette player, chainsaw, church, French horn, garbage truck, gas pump, golf ball, parachute. Response with only the correct class without any other text.*''
Achieving better-than-random accuracy (10%) on this task means that D2L can zero-shot transfer visual information to a text-only LLM.


We find that D2L can communicate visual information extracted by the VLM directly into the parameters of the target model. Specifically, the target model achieves 75.03% accuracy on the 10-class Imagenette dataset purely through internalized information. This is a striking result given that D2L and the target LLM have never seen information from any other modalities except text. 

|                                 | SQuAD |  DROP | ROPES |   Imagenette  |
|---------------------------------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-------------:|
| D2L (LLM $\Rightarrow$ LLM) | 0.814 | 0.655 | 0.906 | N/A |
| D2L (VLM $\Rightarrow$ LLM) | 0.705 | 0.568 | 0.772 |    75.03\%    |

These results show the robustness of the proposed D2L across model sizes and families. Remarkably, the proposed architecture is robust enough to zero-shot internalize visual information from a VLM to a pure-text LLM, allowing the target LLM to classify images based purely on the internalized information.

> The baseline may be missed. This work does not compare the performance with other text-to-weight works.

Thank you to the reviewer for the suggestion. We’d like to note that we have used Text-to-LoRA (T2L) as a text-to-weight baseline in our initial submission. Nonetheless, we have added ***Generative Adapter as another text-to-weight baseline for the Mistral-7B model (Appendix E, Figure 9 and 10***). D2L still performs best among the in-parameter methods with minimal memory footprint and sub-second latency.

> It is not clear how the performance is on the distribution dataset. For example, if you train on PwC and test on SQuAD, what is the performance?

We thank the reviewer for the question. We’d like to note that the long-context datasets included in the submitted manuscripts are all OOD for D2L in terms of the context lengths and the distributions of the documents (Section 5.1.2).

Nonetheless, to further challenge the robustness of D2L, we included a data ablation study by ***training D2L with only the data derived from the pre-training corpus in Appendix D*** of the revised paper. We can see that the overall performance of D2L without QA data is comparable to the default training setup. Notably, it slightly outperforms the default D2L on SQuAD and ROPES, while underperforming significantly on DROP due to differences in training data distributions. Regardless of the QA data, D2L consistently outperforms low-budget CD across datasets, suggesting that D2L is largely robust and not highly sensitive to the training data format.

|                     | SQuAD |  DROP | ROPES |
|---------------------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| D2l               | 0.814 | 0.655 | 0.906 |
| D2L w/o QA data | 0.839 | 0.575 | 0.923 |
| CD                 | 0.689 | 0.504 | 0.776 |

---

*We believe these inclusions resolve the concerns regarding the generality of our proposed method, coverage of the baselines, and ablation of the training data raised by the reviewer. We would highly appreciate it if the reviewer could confirm that the concerns have been addressed. If so, we’d like to ask the reviewer to consider increasing the recommendation score. We are happy to discuss further if any additional questions arise.*

summary.value: This paper proposes Doc-to-LoRA,  a hypernetwork that transforms a document into a LoRA. The objective is to produce a LoRA that mimics the behavior of the model with the document in context. The authors claim that this outperforms context distillation in both cost and quality.

strengths.value:
- This paper addresses an important problem: how to reduce the memory consumption of in-context learning over large documents.
- The D2L method is simple and intuitive.
- Can extend the context length of the model 4x on the NIAH task. This result is very interesting!
- Compared with context distillation, it has significantly lower internalization cost.
- Well-written and easy to follow

weaknesses.value:
- The main claim of the paper is that D2L “outperforms CD with improved internalization
efficiency.” This claim lacks nuance and is incautious. [Prior work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266) shows that performance of context distillation improves steadily as you increase the number of generated queries (up to hundreds of thousands of queries). However the authors compare against CD with only 5 generated queries for context distillation. Given this, the broad claim that D2L outperforms CD both in efficiency and quality lacks evidence. From the results presented in the paper, I am not convinced that D2L categorically outperforms CD in quality, it depends on how many generated queries we use. Indeed, [Prior work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266) has shown that CD can match the performance of the full context on the QASPER dataset, while D2L cannot in Figure 4.
    - So, my main concern with this paper is that it makes an absolute comparison between CD and D2L instead of discussing the cost-quality tradeoff between the two approaches. The evidence seems to suggest that CD still can significantly outperform D2L on long context tasks when we increase the number of generated queries.
    - Without a revision that explores these tradeoffs and presents more nuanced claims, I can’t recommend acceptance. With a more nuanced analysis of these tradeoffs and comparisons with more generated queries, I would raise my score.
    - I would recommend that the authors frame D2L and CD as complementary methods. The best method to use may depend on the setting and computational constraint. I could even imagine using D2L to initialize CD and speedup convergence.
- It is unclear how D2L performs relative to other existing hypernetwork-based methods such as Gisting, MEND, autocompressors, or in-context AutoEncoders. Text2Lora is the only hypernetwork based method compared against.
- Unlike recently proposed methods based on CD (*e.g.* https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266), D2L cannot match the performance of the full context.
    - D2LThe authors could also evaluate D2L on more challenging document understanding datasets that evaluate capabilities beyond QA. Some that come to mind are: FinanceBench, LongHealth, and Machine-translation from one book. Prior work in context distillation evaluate on these
- D2L interferes significantly with existing internal knowledge in the base LLM. [Existing context distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266) methods do not exhibit forgetting. It is possible that improving the meta-learning data generation pipeline, but the authors do not demonstrate this in this paper.
- The main difference between doc-to-Lora and prior work, text-to-Lora, lies in the distribution of context-query pairs used to train the hyper network. Given this, I would expect a description of the training distribution to feature prominently in Section 3, which describes the method. Instead, the data is only briefly described in the experimental setup section. Specifically, I’d like to better understand what prompts are used to generate the queries.
- There are a number of important questions left unanswered. See below.

questions.value:
- Can the same strategy be used to produce a truncated key-value cache (instead of a LoRA), as in [prefix-tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00190) and [cartridges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266)?
- How do the authors justify the choice of the perceiver architecture? What are the alternatives and how does performance differ?
- How does performance vary as you increase the rank of the LoRA adapter?
- Why does the model OOM with 40 context distillation queries? By keeping batch size constant, context distillation can be scaled to an arbitrarily large number of training queries. (*e.g. in [cartridges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266)* the authors scale to >100k context distillation queries).

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for commenting on the paper as being ***simple and intuitive*** and that the paper ***addresses an important problem***. We are delighted to hear that the ***NIAH result is very interesting*** and ***D2L has significantly lower internalization cost compared to CD***. We provide further clarification and address the existing concerns of the reviewer below.

> The main claim of the paper is that D2L “outperforms CD with improved internalization efficiency.” This claim lacks nuance and is incautious. Prior work shows that performance of context distillation improves steadily as you increase the number of generated queries. However the authors compare against CD with only 5 generated queries for context distillation. Given this, the broad claim that D2L outperforms CD both in efficiency and quality lacks evidence. From the results presented in the paper, I am not convinced that D2L categorically outperforms CD in quality, it depends on how many generated queries we use. 

> So, my main concern with this paper is that it makes an absolute comparison between CD and D2L instead of discussing the cost-quality tradeoff between the two approaches. The evidence seems to suggest that CD still can significantly outperform D2L on long context tasks when we increase the number of generated queries.

> Without a revision that explores these tradeoffs and presents more nuanced claims, I can’t recommend acceptance. With a more nuanced analysis of these tradeoffs and comparisons with more generated queries, I would raise my score.

We thank the reviewer for carefully reading the paper and noticing the mismatch between our CD baseline and a prior work (Cartridges). The “Prior work” mentioned (Cartridges) uses KV cache (prefix-tuning) parameterization with high capacities (**a few hundreds of MBs to a few GBs of KV cache**) in order to match the performance of ICL. In contrast, our paper focuses on latency- and memory-efficient rank-8 LoRA parameterization (**< 10MB**). Prior work has demonstrated that prefix-tuning is more effective at distilling context than LoRA, even with matching memory footprints. **Therefore, the CD baseline and D2L—parameterized as rank-8 LoRA—are expected to be weaker than even the smallest Cartridges, which cannot match the ICL baseline**. By parameterizing as LoRA, we envision D2L as a step towards practical continual and lifelong learning, where the model can continuously acquire new knowledge through LoRA adapters and is not limited by its context length.

We agree with the reviewer that D2L does not categorically outperform CD on arbitrary tasks or on heavy compute budgets. D2L is trained specifically for QA tasks, while CD is a general method. CD can benefit from utilizing more generated queries. We are aware of this tradeoff and show in Table 4 and 5 (Section 6) that D2L likely has learned a specialized but biased form of CD, assuming that the queries are from QA tasks and are related to the internalized context. Furthermore, Table 4 shows that CD indeed benefits from using more generated queries. ***Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have refined the text and experimental descriptions throughout the revised paper to emphasize these nuances.***

comment.value:
To clearly address the concern regarding the low-budget CD, we provide our reasoning and justifications below. We use a small number of queries for CDs for two reasons:
- **Update latency:** First, our primary interest lies in scenarios where update latency is a critical factor. Notable examples include updating local LLMs on consumer-grade GPUs or edge devices. Furthermore, low-latency adaptation is essential for rapidly evolving environments, such as active codebases or agentic tasks. Our CD baseline typically requires approximately 1-2 minutes for convergence on a single H200 GPU. In contrast, D2L generates a context-specific LoRA within a single forward pass, which takes less than one second and can be executed on consumer-grade hardware, as it demands significantly less VRAM ($<$10GB) compared to the memory requirements of low-budget CD (40-80GB). While we concur that increasing the number of queries could enhance CD performance, the central thesis of this paper is that D2L can instantly internalize new knowledge into the model parameters. In contrast, conventional CD requires several minutes, even with a limited number of queries.
- **Evaluation coverage:** The second reason for using a few queries is that we want to evaluate all methods across a large amount of documents (**we use more than two thousand document instances across 6 datasets**) to rigorously challenge the robustness of trained D2L. We observe that it takes around 12 hours to evaluate CD even with just 20 queries on 500 samples from the SQuAD dataset. Consequently, evaluating CD with larger numbers of queries would be computationally prohibitive, particularly if we are to maintain the comprehensive evaluation coverage included in our submission.

Nonetheless, we have ***updated Table 4 with mini-batch CD updates up to 100 queries per context*** (previously up to 30) on a 100-document subset of the SQuAD dataset and contextualize the update latency of when using CD with increasing numbers of queries.


| Method                     | Normalized Performance | Update Latency (s)    |
|----------------------------|------------------------|-----------------------|
| CD (oracle)                | 0.988                  | 8.763 $\pm$ 0.313     |
| D2L                        | **0.866**              | **0.086** $\pm$ 0.061 |
| CD (100 generated queries) | 0.650                  | 631.101 $\pm$ 12.879  |
| CD (50 generated queries)  | 0.601                  | 311.661 $\pm$ 7.211   |
| CD (20 generated queries)  | 0.506                  | 129.044 $\pm$ 5.813   |

Also, we have included CD with 25 queries (previously only 5) on all long-context benchmarks (***Table 1,8,9***). We refer to the updated tables in the revised manuscript. We provide the updated result on the 2WikiMultihopQA here. 


| Method                                    | Normalized Performance($\uparrow$) | Additional Update Memory (GB, $\downarrow$) | Mean Update Latency (s, $\downarrow$) |
|-------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| CD (oracle query)                         | 0.901                            | 7.820                                     | 40.171 $\pm$ 0.351                  |
| D2L (batched)                             | **0.857**                        | 11.522                                    | **0.209** $\pm$ 0.123               |
| D2L (iterative)                           | 0.844                            | **3.791**                                 | 0.551 $\pm$ 0.101                   |
| **CD (25 generated queries, mini-batch SGD, NEW)** | 0.745                            | 59.925                                    | 465.454 $\pm$ 67.868                |
| CD (5 generated queries, full-batch SGD)  | 0.704                            | 79.371                                    | 72.537 $\pm$ 7.821                  |

As pointed out by the reviewer, CD performs better as the query budget increases. Although increasing the budget to hundreds or thousands of queries would likely boost CD performance beyond that of D2L, the update latency would also increase substantially. Such a large latency would render the user experience non-responsive, especially in fast-changing environments, e.g., active codebases or agentic tasks. *These results highlight the effectiveness of D2L at instantly internalizing knowledge in the sub-second regime.*
Finally, we want to emphasize that a direct comparison with Cartridges is not applicable, as D2L utilizes a much smaller internalization parameterization (rank-8 LoRA, which consumes less than 10MB of VRAM) and focuses on internalization efficiency and speed.

> I would recommend that the authors frame D2L and CD as complementary methods. The best method to use may depend on the setting and computational constraint. I could even imagine using D2L to initialize CD and speedup convergence.

We also agree that combining D2L with CD could be beneficial in terms of convergence speed and potentially improved performance. However, due to the limited time of the rebuttal period, we did not investigate the combined approach. Nonetheless, we have added and discussed this combination in the Limitations section.

> It is unclear how D2L performs relative to other existing hypernetwork-based methods such as Gisting, MEND, autocompressors, or in-context AutoEncoders. Text2Lora is the only hypernetwork based method compared against.

Thank you to the reviewer for the suggestion. We have added ***two new target models (Mistral-7B and Qwen3-4B) in Appendix E (Figure 9-12)*** in the revised paper. We have added ***Generative Adapter as another hypernetwork-based baseline for a new target model, Mistral-7B (Appendix E, Figure 9 and 10***). D2L still performs best among the in-parameter methods with minimal memory footprint and sub-second latency. These results show the robustness of the proposed D2L across model sizes and families. We hope that the inclusion of the new baseline resolves the reviewer's concern regarding comparison with existing hypernetwork-based methods.


> Unlike recently proposed methods based on CD (e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266), D2L cannot match the performance of the full context.

We would like to reiterate that the paper mentioned (Cartridges) employs a high-capacity prefix-tuning parameterization (a few hundred MBs to a few GBs) in order to match the performance of ICL. The smallest Cartridge size reported (~150MB) **does not match** the performance of the ICL baseline. Therefore, the rank-8 LoRA (<10MB) parameterization used in our work is expected to also be less performant than the ICL baseline. 

> The authors could also evaluate D2L on more challenging document understanding datasets that evaluate capabilities beyond QA. Some that come to mind are: FinanceBench, LongHealth, and Machine-translation from one book. Prior work in context distillation evaluate on these

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. First, we would like to clarify the experimental rigor required to produce the results presented in the submission. The prior work mentioned (Cartridges) evaluates on FinanceBench, LongHealth, and Machine-translation with only ***4 document instances***. D2L, on the other hand, is evaluated on ***more than two thousand document instances across 6 different datasets***. Additionally, our NIAH experiment comprises thousands of test samples. Furthermore, our submission includes an extreme generalization test (Table 3, Section 6), where D2L has to internalize queries instead of document information. We believe that these results are collectively diverse and challenging for D2L, shedding light on how D2L might generalize beyond QA tasks.

> D2L interferes significantly with existing internal knowledge in the base LLM. Existing context distillation methods do not exhibit forgetting. It is possible that improving the meta-learning data generation pipeline, but the authors do not demonstrate this in this paper.

We agree that knowledge interference is a significant problem and mention it explicitly in our paper. Compared to prefix-tuning (KV cache) used in the Cartridges paper, LoRA is found to be more destructive. As a result, our Knowledge Interference experiment in Section 6 is simply a test for the current implementation of D2L without a dedicated knowledge preservation mechanism and serves as a baseline for future work to improve upon. We agree with the reviewer that using prefix-tuning parameterization (as in Cartridges) could help mitigate this problem. We have updated the text accordingly to discuss potential dedicated mechanisms and clarify the focus of the experiment.

> The main difference between doc-to-Lora and prior work, text-to-Lora, lies in the distribution of context-query pairs used to train the hyper network. Given this, I would expect a description of the training distribution to feature prominently in Section 3, which describes the method. Instead, the data is only briefly described in the experimental setup section. Specifically, I’d like to better understand what prompts are used to generate the queries.

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity of the training data and the data generation process. We apologize that this information was unclear in the initial submission. The information was included in the Appendix initially due to the page limit constraint. In the revised submission, we have added a new section (Section 5.2) dedicated to describing the data generation pipeline used for the training of D2L. We briefly describe the process here:

- **Data Sources:** The training dataset combines a subset of **FineWeb-Edu** with several standard **QA datasets** (PwC, SQuAD, ROPES, and DROP). These QA datasets come with (context, query, response) triplets.
- **Synthetic Query Generation (FineWeb-Edu):**
  - For the FineWeb-Edu texts, a larger model (gemma-3-12b-it) generated **10 questions** per context to ensure high quality.
  - This was done in **two iterations** (5 questions each). The second iteration reviewed the first set to ensure new questions were distinct and more challenging.
  - We refer to Listings 4 and 5 in the Appendix for the prompts used to generate the queries
  - The answers generated during this specific step were discarded.
- **Instruction Formatting:** The queries were wrapped into random instruction templates (applied to all data except PwC).
- **Target Response Generation:**
  - The target model (gemma-2-2b-it) generates a single response for every unique context-query pair.
  - The **top-16 logit values** for every token in these responses were recorded to serve as the final training targets.


> Can the same strategy be used to produce a truncated key-value cache (instead of a LoRA), as in prefix-tuning and cartridges?

We thank the reviewer for the question. Yes, we believe that D2L can be modified to output other parameterizations, such as prefix-tuning as used by Cartridges. We focus on LoRA parameterization in this submission because it is commonly used by practitioners. Our submission is a proof-of-concept of a framework that meta-learns CD effectively. We believe that incorporating prefix-tuning into the current framework could improve performance and even help mitigate the knowledge interference problem. We will explore such parameterization and others in future work.

> How do the authors justify the choice of the perceiver architecture? What are the alternatives and how does performance differ?

We thank the reviewer for the question. The Perceiver architecture is a general and powerful architecture that maps sequences of arbitrary lengths (i.e., context text) into a fixed-size output (i.e., LoRA matrices). It has been demonstrated to effectively tackle high-dimensional problems. Based on our research, Perceiver seems to be the most flexible yet powerful architecture that is effective at utilizing GPUs during training (compared to RNN-style networks that cannot be parallelized). Other architectures with the right inductive biases for weight generations could perform better than Perceiver. However, in our proof-of-concept submission, we believe that Perceiver serves as a strong and simple baseline for meta-learning CD.
One recent alternative is to use the outer product of the context token activations, following the Generative Adapter [2]. However, this alternative assumes that the context encoder must share the exact same architecture as the target model. It also requires initialization tricks to train steadily. On the other hand, Perceiver enables us to explore unconventional experiments, such as internalizing visual information into a pure-text LLM, thanks to Perceiver’s generality.

> How does performance vary as you increase the rank of the LoRA adapter?

Thank you to the reviewer for the question. We have included a new result with increased LoRA rank in ***Appendix E (Table 8)***. In particular, we increased the rank of the LoRA from 8 to 16. We opt to use rank-8 LoRA for the main experiments for ease of running experiments (less VRAM and faster training).

summary.value: Several works have been exploring test-time-training and context distillation methods to compress key-value caches into a small number of learned weights. However, the training step needs to be re-done for each new context, which is slow and expensive. This work explores whether a hypernetwork that goes from the context to the compressed weights directly. The work explores the architecture and training protocol to accomplish this and performs a series of short and long context benchmark evaluations.

strengths.value:
The project is well-motivated and clearly contextualized within the literature
It is interesting if it’s possible to create a hypernetwork that replaces the process of running gradient descent. 
The chosen architecture makes sense and is clearly explained
The paper chooses a comprehensive set of evaluation settings / benchmark tasks

L076-079: The writing could be clarified: Why is chunking needed? Why is NIAH the right evaluation for success? Why is training limited to 256 tokens? 
L140-142: What type of data was used in the meta-training dataset? What was the process for generating the context, queries, and responses

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for commenting on the paper as being ***well-motivated*** and ***clearly contextualized within the literature***. We are happy to hear that the ***architecture makes sense***, ***is clearly explained***, and that the paper includes ***a comprehensive set of evaluation settings/benchmark tasks***.

We provide further clarification and address the existing concerns of the reviewer below.

---

> Why is chunking needed? 

We thank the reviewer for the question. The chunking mechanism is needed for internalizing documents that are longer than the context window of the context encoder. For instance, gemma-2-2b-it only has a context window length of 8192 tokens, beyond which the model's behavior becomes unpredictable. Therefore, internalizing documents longer than 8192 tokens needs chunking to ensure that the context encoder operates under its well-behaved regime. We have updated the text to clarify this point.

> Why is NIAH the right evaluation for success?

We thank the reviewer for the question. NIAH is a classic and established task for evaluating long-context understanding capabilities and is part of various long-context benchmarks. Therefore, we use it as a pedagogical example to clearly demonstrate the benefits and effectiveness of D2L. D2L effectively internalizes the needle information and achieves near-perfect zero-shot accuracy on contexts beyond 32K tokens, while removing all context information from the target LLM's context window. Furthermore, we use various additional benchmarks (SQuAD, DROP, ROPES, 2WikiMultihopQA, MultiFieldQA, QASPER) to validate our approach on real-world tasks.


> Why is training limited to 256 tokens? 

We thank the reviewer for the question. We aim to demonstrate that D2L is capable of generalizing beyond the lengths of its training data and that the chunking mechanism functions as intended. Additionally, training on shorter lengths is significantly faster due to the quadratic growth of the attention mechanism. Therefore, we use shorter context lengths for the training data of the NIAH task. We have updated the text accordingly.


> What type of data was used in the meta-training dataset?

> What was the process for generating the context, queries, and responses?

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity of the training data and the data generation process. We apologize that this information was unclear in the initial submission. The information was included in the Appendix initially due to the page limit constraint. In the revised submission, we have added a new section (Section 5.2) dedicated to describing the data generation pipeline used for the training of D2L. We briefly describe the process here:

- **Data Sources:** The training dataset combines a subset of **FineWeb-Edu** with several standard **QA datasets** (PwC, SQuAD, ROPES, and DROP). These QA datasets come with (context, query, response) triplets.
- **Synthetic Query Generation (FineWeb-Edu):**
  - For the FineWeb-Edu texts, a larger model (gemma-3-12b-it) generated **10 questions** per context to ensure high quality.
  - This was done in **two iterations** (5 questions each). The second iteration reviewed the first set to ensure new questions were distinct and more challenging.
  - We refer to Listings 4 and 5 in the Appendix for the prompts used to generate the queries
  - The answers generated during this specific step were discarded.
- **Instruction Formatting:** The queries were wrapped into random instruction templates (applied to all data except PwC).
- **Target Response Generation:**
  - The target model (gemma-2-2b-it) generates a single response for every unique context-query pair.
  - The **top-16 logit values** for every token in these responses were recorded to serve as the final training targets.

> Why include samples from the QA datasets? Especially since those are also the chosen evaluation settings.

> Are the samples that you test on in the training data as well?

> How does the method perform on OOD datasets?

> How does the method perform on SQAD/DROP/ROPES if their samples are not included in the training data? 

> Why not just use the pretraining corpus? 


We thank the reviewer for paying such attention to the training data and evaluation benchmarks. We include samples from the QA datasets to ensure that D2L learns to respond correctly to the question formats presented in those datasets. We confirm that the test samples in the benchmarks are entirely unseen. We also like to highlight that the *long-context benchmarks are OOD for D2L in terms of the context lengths and the distributions of the documents (Section 5.1.2)*.

Nonetheless, to further challenge the robustness of D2L, we included a data ablation study by ***training D2L with only the data derived from the pre-training corpus in Appendix D (Table 7)*** of the revised paper. We can see that the overall performance of D2L without QA data is comparable to the default training setup. Notably, it slightly outperforms the default D2L on SQuAD and ROPES, while underperforming significantly on DROP due to differences in training data distributions. Regardless of the QA data, D2L consistently outperforms low-budget CD across datasets, suggesting that D2L is largely robust and not highly sensitive to the training data format.

|                     | SQuAD |  DROP | ROPES |
|---------------------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| D2l               | 0.814 | 0.655 | 0.906 |
| D2L w/o QA data | 0.839 | 0.575 | 0.923 |
| CD                 | 0.689 | 0.504 | 0.776 |



> What is meant by CD OOMs? 

> Don’t prior works like Cartridges evaluate on documents up to 100-400K tokens? Why can’t you chunking the context to avoid OOMs during training (since some of your baseline papers do that)? 

We thank the reviewer for the question. In our initial submission, we used full-batch SGD for CD. That is, all the query-response pairs are used to compute the gradient of each optimizer step. This is an artifact in our implementation. We have now updated the results so that mini-batch SGD is used for CD with larger numbers of queries (***Table 1,4,8,9***). The overall interpretation of the results still stands. D2L consistently outperforms low-budget CD with significant memory saved and orders-of-magnitude speedup, making effective sub-second adaptation possible.


> What is the GPU type being used / setup?

All evaluations and measurements are done with a single H200 GPU. We set the maximum number of test samples in each dataset to be 500 due to the high overhead latency of CD (even with small numbers of queries). We use the same query template for all the benchmarks except for QASPER (see Listing 8). We include this information in Appendix B.

> Why is it meaningful to compare to CD with 5 queries? This claim is not clearly supported and this experiment doesn’t make sense to me. 

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the small number of queries used for CD. For clarification, we use 20 queries per context for the QA datasets (SQuAD, DROP, ROPES) and 5 queries per context for the long-context QA tasks (2WikiMultihopQA, MultiFieldQA, QASPER). We want to clarify the use of fewer queries in this context. We use a small number of queries for CDs for two reasons:
- **Update latency:** First, our primary interest lies in scenarios where update latency is a critical factor. Notable examples include updating local LLMs on consumer-grade GPUs or edge devices. Furthermore, low-latency adaptation is essential for rapidly evolving environments, such as active codebases or agentic tasks. Our CD baseline typically requires approximately 1-2 minutes for convergence on a single H200 GPU. In contrast, D2L generates a context-specific LoRA within a single forward pass, which takes less than one second and can be executed on consumer-grade hardware, as it demands significantly less VRAM ($<$10GB) compared to the memory requirements of low-budget CD (40-80GB). While we concur that increasing the number of queries could enhance CD performance, the central thesis of this paper is that D2L can instantly internalize new knowledge into the model parameters. In contrast, conventional CD requires several minutes, even with a limited number of queries.
- **Evaluation coverage:** The second reason for using a few queries is that we want to evaluate all methods across a large amount of documents (**we use more than two thousand document instances across 6 datasets**) to rigorously challenge the robustness of trained D2L. We observe that it takes around 12 hours to evaluate CD even with just 20 queries on 500 samples from the SQuAD dataset. Consequently, evaluating CD with a significantly greater number of queries would be computationally prohibitive, particularly if we are to maintain the comprehensive evaluation coverage included in our submission.

Nonetheless, we have since included ***two new results***.

First, we have included CD with 25 queries (previously 5) on all long-context benchmarks (***Table 1,8,9***). We refer to the updated tables in the revised manuscript. We provide the updated result on the 2WikiMultihopQA here. 

| Method                                    | Normalized Performance($\uparrow$) | Additional Update Memory (GB, $\downarrow$) | Mean Update Latency (s, $\downarrow$) |
|-------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| CD (oracle query)                         | 0.901                            | 7.820                                     | 40.171 $\pm$ 0.351                  |
| D2L (batched)                             | **0.857**                        | 11.522                                    | **0.209** $\pm$ 0.123               |
| D2L (iterative)                           | 0.844                            | **3.791**                                 | 0.551 $\pm$ 0.101                   |
| **CD (25 generated queries, mini-batch SGD, NEW)** | 0.745                            | 59.925                                    | 465.454 $\pm$ 67.868                |
| CD (5 generated queries, full-batch SGD)  | 0.704                            | 79.371                                    | 72.537 $\pm$ 7.821                  |



Second, we have improved the results of our analysis (***Section 6, Table 4***) to include larger numbers of queries up to 100 queries per context (previously 30) and contextualize the update latency of when using CD with increasing numbers of queries.

| Method                     | Normalized Performance | Update Latency (s)    |
|----------------------------|------------------------|-----------------------|
| CD (oracle)                | 0.988                  | 8.763 $\pm$ 0.313     |
| D2L                        | **0.866**              | **0.086** $\pm$ 0.061 |
| CD (100 generated queries) | 0.650                  | 631.101 $\pm$ 12.879  |
| CD (50 generated queries)  | 0.601                  | 311.661 $\pm$ 7.211   |
| CD (20 generated queries)  | 0.506                  | 129.044 $\pm$ 5.813   |


We would like to mention again that, although increasing the budget to hundreds or thousands of queries would likely boost CD performance beyond that of D2L, the update latency would also increase substantially. Such a large latency would render the user experience non-responsive, especially in fast-changing environments, e.g., active codebases, or agentic tasks. *These results highlight the effectiveness of D2L at instantly internalizing knowledge in the sub-second regime.*

> It would be more compelling to present scaling laws. How quickly does D2L performance increase as a function of training data? What properties of the training data led to this performance.


We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We have since added a new result showing the learning curves of D2L (***Appendix D, Figure 6***). The plot can be accessed online [here](https://imgur.com/a/Gi9ROCF). We take various checkpoints of D2L and continue training with 1,000 optimizer steps, using a linear decay learning rate following the Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) approach.

We can see that D2L trains steadily, performing better at QA tasks as it sees more training samples. We attribute the success of D2L to the diverse synthetic training data from the pre-train corpus, which enables D2L to generalize well even when no QA datasets are used for training (cf. new results in ***Appendix D, Table 7***).


> What does it mean to internalize a query and what is the motivation for the experiment?


We thank the reviewer for pointing out the gap in our experimental description. In our Query Internalization experiment (Section 6), we aim to test the robustness of D2L, specifically whether it can be used to internalize information beyond factual information from documents. To answer this question, we use the existing SQuAD dataset with a slight modification. Instead of internalizing the document, we use D2L to internalize the query. This means that, during evaluation, the target model sees the document directly but not the query. The results show that the target model still mostly behaves by attempting to answer the internalized query. This result is encouraging and suggests that D2L can function properly under such an extreme generalization test.

The motivation for the experiment comes from Askell et al. [1], who show that simple system prompts can be effectively internalized through CD to steer the behavior of LLMs. The Query Internalization experiment is analogous to a setting where we could use D2L for internalizing system prompts before deployment, thereby saving precious space in the context window of LLMs.

We have updated the text to clarify these points.

---

*We believe the inclusion of new results and clarifications resolve all concerns and questions raised by the reviewer. We would highly appreciate it if the reviewer could confirm that the concerns have been addressed. If so, we’d like to ask the reviewer to consider increasing the recommendation score. We are happy to discuss further if any additional questions arise.*

References

[1] Askell et al. "A general language assistant as a laboratory for alignment." arXiv preprint (2021).

summary.value:
The paper proposes Doc-to-LoRA, a hypernetwork that transforms a document into a LoRA. The objective is to produce a LoRA that mimics the behavior of the model with the document in context. 

The reviewers were generally positive about the research direction. They raised the following main concerns: 
1. Reviewer x6RM asked for missing baselines (existing hypernetwork-based methods such as Gisting, MEND, autocompressors; also reviewer 8n1Y and x6RM). Reviewer also asked to see results on another model family and on OOD settings. 
2. Reviewer 8n1Y raised concerns about the cost-quality tradeoffs. Particularly, they point out that prior approach CD's implementation in this work uses an orders of magnitude less queries than recommended, leading to a much worse performing baseline.
They asked for clarifications on how this method is substantially different from previous text-to-lora methods. 
Finally, they raised the concern that while some prior works are able to match the full-context performance, D2L cannot. They also question whether D2L causes catastrophic forgetting. 
3. Reviewer xX1k shares some concerns with the above two, particularly OOD performance, and the implementation of the prior baseline that uses a much higher number of queries than in this paper.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The rebuttal addressed the clarifications questions asked by Reviewer xX1k. It also reported results on other models, and showed that the performance improvements hold on these model families. 
The rebuttal also included more analysis of the cost-quality tradeoff, showing that the prior baseline significantly underperformed D2L even with 100 queries. However, this is still lower than the recommended paper. 

Major outstanding issues:
I am not convinced that the rebuttal addressed the OOD performance concern. Specifically, the reviewers asked to see OOD performance for very specific datasets (PwC -> Squad) which was not directly reported. 
A number of reviewer 8n1Y's concerns were not convincingly addressed -- particularly, the rebuttal does not justify why their method cannot match full-context performance similar to baselines. The rebuttal also does not include comparisons with text-to-lora baselines explicitly requested.

reviewer_scores.value:
Reviewer x6RM would have increased their score from 4-->6. 
I believe reviewers 8n1Y and xX1k would have maintained their scores.
